# Results — Study 1017 (Do Bull Markets Die of Old Age?) on the real tapes

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). As-of **2022-11-30** (FF monthly to
**2018-11-30**, S&P daily to **2022-11-30** — the partial December 2022 is dropped).
Fingerprints: FF `394be76d78ac`, S&P `e223c581ae22`. 1,000 null paths per null model
(400 for the sensitivity rows), 2,000 cycle-bootstrap draws.*

| Fama-French monthly (total return) | arch (bundled) · frenchdata.csv.gz · Fama-French Mkt-RF + RF, monthly, percent | `f23436727b01d879…` | total return, nominal, USD | 2018-11-30 |

index** (no dividends): an out-of-sample cross-check with daily resolution and few cycles.

## 1. The bull markets

Conventional rule: a bull ends when the index falls 20% below its high; a bear ends when it rises
20% above its low; turning points are the extremes in between. Monthly closes on the total-return
index. The first partial phase (from the July 1926 sample start) is dropped — its start is unknown.

| Trough | Peak | Months | Gain | Peak confirmed |
|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| 1932-06 | 1932-08 | 2 | +84% | 1932-11 | |
| 1933-02 | 1937-02 | 48 | +280% | 1937-09 | |
| 1938-03 | 1940-04 | 25 | +65% | 1940-05 | |
| 1940-05 | 1941-07 | 14 | +20% | 1942-04 | |
| 1942-04 | 1946-05 | 49 | +229% | 1946-09 | |
| 1947-05 | 1961-12 | 175 | +843% | 1962-06 | |
| 1962-06 | 1968-11 | 77 | +160% | 1970-01 | |
| 1970-06 | 1972-12 | 30 | +76% | 1973-11 | |
| 1974-09 | 1987-08 | 155 | +925% | 1987-10 | |
| 1987-11 | 2000-08 | 153 | +783% | 2001-02 | |
| 2002-09 | 2007-10 | 61 | +117% | 2008-09 | |
| 2009-02 | 2018-11 | 117 | +368% | — | running (censored) |

**11 completed bulls** in 92 years (plus the one still running in
November 2018, right-censored). That is the whole sample — and the honest constraint on everything
below. The median completed bull ran **49 months**; the median bear
12. A peak is only *known* once the index is 20% below it: the median
confirmation came **5.9 months** after the top.

## 2. The hazard by age — real bulls against random-walk bulls

Life table: the probability that a bull which has reached a given age ends within the following
year. The real column rests on 12 spells; the null columns pool
1,000 simulated tapes of the same length dated with the same rule.

| Bull age | At risk | Ended | Censored | Real: P(end within a year) | Random walk | GARCH(1,1)-t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0–1y | 12 | 1 | 0 | **8%** | 16% | 24% |
| 1–2y | 11 | 1 | 0 | **9%** | 23% | 19% |
| 2–3y | 10 | 2 | 0 | **20%** | 22% | 14% |
| 3–5y | 8 | 2 | 0 | **13%** | 22% | 12% |
| 5–8y | 6 | 2 | 0 | **13%** | 23% | 12% |
| 8y+ | 4 | 3 | 1 | **15%** | 23% | 12% |

The real hazard does rise from the first year to the third — exactly the shape the believers
point to. But a dating rule that needs a 20% move to start and a 20% fall to end a bull also gives
a random walk a low first-year hazard. The real hazard after year three is *flat to falling*, not
rising.

## 3. The Weibull shape against the null

| | Shape k | 90% band / 95% CI | p (H₁: real ages faster) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **Real bulls (±20%)** | **1.10** | 0.72–2.00 (cycle bootstrap, 95%) | — |
| Naive test of k = 1 (likelihood ratio) | | | 0.70 |
| Random walk, μ = 0.0079, σ = 0.0531 / month | 1.22 | 0.94–1.74 | **0.72** |
| GARCH(1,1)-t (α = 0.133, β = 0.831, ν = 6.6), same drift | 0.91 | 0.63–1.55 | **0.24** |

Two things are true at once. **The dating rule manufactures ageing**: 88%
of pure random walks dated this way show k > 1 (median 1.22), and the naive
likelihood-ratio test would call a memoryless random walk "dies of old age" on
18% of paths. And **real bulls age no faster than that**: the real k of
1.10 sits *below* the random-walk median, at p = 0.72. Against GARCH — where
volatility clustering produces long calm bulls and a falling hazard (median k
0.91) — the real k is higher, but at p = 0.24, nowhere near a
test. Real bulls are fewer and longer than random-walk bulls (11 vs a median
16 per tape; median length 49 vs
35 months), closer to the GARCH world (12
bulls, median 41 months) — long, calm expansions are a
volatility-regime fact, not an ageing fact.

## 4. Sensitivity to the dating rule

| Rule | Completed bulls | Median (months) | Real k | 95% CI | RW null k | p (RW) | GARCH null k | p (GARCH) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| ±15% | 20 | 28 | **0.96** | 0.73–1.50 | 1.23 | 0.97 | 0.91 | 0.38 |
| ±20% | 11 | 49 | **1.10** | 0.72–2.00 | 1.22 | 0.72 | 0.91 | 0.24 |
| ±25% | 8 | 54 | **0.92** | 0.58–1.97 | 1.20 | 0.91 | 0.92 | 0.49 |
| +20% / −15% (asymmetric) | 18 | 30 | **1.09** | 0.81–1.79 | 1.32 | 0.91 | 0.96 | 0.25 |

The asymmetric row ends bulls on a 15% fall but needs a 20% rise to start one, a filter in the
spirit of Lunde & Timmermann (2004). No rule produces real ageing beyond both nulls.

## 5. Does the age of the bull predict the next 12 months?

Real-time age (months since the trough that started the current *confirmed* bull, using only data
to date), in years; months in a confirmed bull only; overlapping 12-month windows.

| Target | Slope per year of age | Newey-West t (18 lags) | Non-overlapping t | Simulated p (RW / GARCH) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Next-12m excess log return | -0.39% | **-0.99** | -0.95 (n = 75) | 0.35 / 0.33 |
| Next-12m max drawdown | -0.16% | -0.69 | -0.05 | — |

The sign leans the believers' way and the size is nothing: a decade of extra age moves the
expected next-year return by about -4%, with t = -0.99
on 898 overlapping months (75 independent ones). Age is a trending,
persistent regressor, so the HAC t is checked against the same regression on random-walk paths: a
random walk yields a t at or below the real one 35% of the time (its median t is
-0.44, its 5th percentile -2.41).

What a de-risker would actually give up — next-month excess return by real-time state (from
1940-05, when three completed bulls first exist to set a median):

| State at month-end | Months | Mean excess (ann.) | Vol | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| young bull (age ≤ median) | 270 | +8.46% | 13.1% | 0.64 |
| old bull (age > median) | 559 | +9.30% | 13.9% | 0.67 |
| bear / unconfirmed | 113 | +2.63% | 20.0% | 0.13 |

Old bulls minus young bulls: **+0.84% a year** (Newey-West t =
+0.24). Late-cycle months did not pay less.

## 6. Could you trade it?

Rule: hold 100% equity, cut to **50% (rest in T-bills)** once the current bull is older than the
median completed bull known at that month-end. One month of lag (weight set at the close of *t*
earns *t+1*), costs one-way × traded NAV, excess-of-cash Sharpe for both legs. Window: from
1940-05 (the rule's first live month) to 2018-11, 78 years,
FF total return.

| Cost | Sharpe B&H | Sharpe rule (gross) | Sharpe rule (net) | Δ net − B&H (95% CI) | p (rule better) | $1 B&H | $1 rule (net) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bp | 0.568 | 0.490 | 0.490 | **-0.077** (-0.163 to +0.008) | 0.963 | $4,787 | $782 |
| 10 bp | 0.568 | 0.490 | 0.489 | **-0.079** (-0.165 to +0.006) | 0.965 | $4,787 | $773 |
| 25 bp | 0.568 | 0.490 | 0.487 | **-0.081** (-0.166 to +0.004) | 0.971 | $4,787 | $761 |

The rule is de-risked in 59% of months (average equity weight
70%, one-way turnover 14% of NAV a year). It cuts vol from
14.5% to 11.2% and trims the worst drawdown only from -50%
to -46% (old bulls do not end in worse crashes than young ones), and it
**lowers** the Sharpe ratio: a costless constant mix with the same
average exposure earns Sharpe 0.568 and $1,079, so the timing itself
subtracts value. Out of sample, on the daily S&P 500 price index 1990 → 2018-11 (median
age seeded with the 48-month median of FF bulls confirmed before
1990, cash = daily-ised T-bill): Sharpe 0.249 net vs 0.336
buy-and-hold, Δ -0.087 (-0.175 to +0.011);
$1 → $4.63 vs $7.67 (price only, dividends excluded on both legs).

## 7. Machinery proof — the harness can see ageing when it is there

Synthetic tape, same length and similar drift/vol, from `data.synthetic_monthly`. At
`signal_strength = 1` bulls older than three years face a planted, rising monthly probability of a
bull-ending crash; at `0` the tape is exactly the random-walk null. Same code path as the real run
(random-walk null only, 200 paths). **Synthetic — not market evidence.**

| signal_strength | Bulls | Real-path k | Null k | p (k) | Prediction t | p (pred) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1.0 | 20 | 2.54 | 1.22 | 0.005 | -3.53 | 0.005 |
| 0.0 | 13 | 1.37 | 1.21 | 0.244 | -0.66 | 0.393 |

The planted world is flagged on both tests; the matched null is not. A null result on the real
tape is therefore a finding about markets, not a blind harness.

## Caveats

- **11 completed bull markets is the whole sample.** The Weibull CI on the real k
  (0.72–2.00) is wide enough to contain both "memoryless" and "ages
  briskly". The null comparison does not create information; it only stops the dating rule from
  being mistaken for a finding. No test on this topic can be powerful with ~12 cycles a century.
- **Monthly closes smooth intramonth extremes.** October 1987 or March 2020 bottoms fall between
  month-ends, which moves some turning points by a month and merges or splits a few short phases
  (the 1932 and 1940–42 episodes sit close to the 20% line). The 15%/25% rows bracket this.
- **The rule is the conventional newspaper one, not a business-cycle algorithm.** We did not
  implement the Pagan–Sossounov (2003) Bry–Boschan-style censoring rules (minimum phase and cycle
  lengths); they would remove the shortest phases, which mechanically raises k on real *and* null
  tapes alike.
- **The S&P cross-check is a price index** (no dividends) and contains only
  6 completed bulls since 1990, two of them
  short bear-market rallies; it is a robustness check of the trading rule, not a second hazard estimate.
- **Bull "age" in the predictive regression is real-time** and starts only once a bull is
  confirmed — up to several months after the trough. Ex-post dated ages would add look-ahead.
- **The nulls are monthly i.i.d. lognormal and GARCH(1,1)-t** with the tape's drift. Neither has
  time-varying expected returns (valuation mean reversion), which is the most plausible channel
  for genuine late-cycle weakness — and which shows up in neither the hazard nor the 12-month
  regression here.

## Verdict

Produced by `strategy.verdict`, thresholds fixed before the real tape was run and unit-tested in
[`tests/test_strategy.py`](../tests/test_strategy.py).

**Signal: None.** Dated with the conventional ±20% rule on 92 years of total-return data, the 11 completed US bull markets have a Weibull shape of **k = 1.10** (cycle-bootstrap 95% CI 0.72–2.00); k > 1 is the textbook signature of "dying of old age". But the ruler produces that by itself. The same rule applied to random walks with the tape's own drift and volatility gives a median **k = 1.22** (GARCH: 0.91), and the real bulls sit at one-sided **p = 0.72** against the random walk and **p = 0.24** against GARCH. Bull age does not forecast the next year either: the slope of the next-12-month excess log return on age is -0.39% per year of age (Newey-West t = **-0.99**, simulated p = 0.35). Real bulls age like random-walk bulls: the apparent senescence is an artefact of the dating rule. Across the 15%, 20%, 25% and asymmetric rules the smallest single-null p-value is 0.24, and the real k never clears both nulls.

**Tradability: Mirage.** Cutting equity to 50% once a bull outlives the median completed bull known at the time (one month lag, 10 bp one-way, bills as cash) changes the excess-of-cash Sharpe from 0.57 (buy-and-hold) to 0.49 net — a gap of -0.08 (block-bootstrap 95% CI -0.16 to +0.01, p = 0.97) — while terminal wealth on $1 goes from $4,787 to $773: the rule spends 59% of months half in bills and simply forgoes the equity premium in old bulls that kept running. On the out-of-sample S&P 500 daily tape (price-only, 1990–2018) the Sharpe gap is -0.09. Nothing to harvest: de-risking old bulls is market timing on noise.

> **In one sentence:** Bull markets only look like they die of old age (Weibull k = 1.10) because a ±20% ruler builds ageing into any series — random walks dated the same way age at least as fast (p = 0.72), bull age does not forecast next year's return (t = -0.99), and selling half of every old bull ended with 6.2× less money than buy-and-hold.
